[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Resilience, Disaster Recovery, and Business Continuity in Cyber Security"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"In modern cyber security, anticipating failures and attacks is just as important as preventing them. While preventive controls reduce risk, they are never 100 percent effective. Organizations must implement robust frameworks for Business Continuity (BC), Disaster Recovery (DR), and Cyber Resilience to ensure operational survival during and after a catastrophic incident."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Core Definitions and Distinctions"},{"order":4,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Business Continuity (BC): The overarching strategy and set of processes that allow an organization to maintain critical functions during and after a major disruption."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Disaster Recovery (DR): A subset of BC focused specifically on the IT and technology infrastructure, detailing how systems, data, and applications are restored."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Cyber Resilience: The ability to continuously deliver expected outcomes despite adverse cyber events by anticipating, withstanding, recovering from, and adapting to attacks."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"Key Metrics: RPO and RTO"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"Designing an effective disaster recovery plan requires defining two crucial recovery metrics:"},{"order":9,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Recovery Point Objective (RPO): The maximum acceptable data loss measured in time. It determines how frequently backups must be performed."},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Recovery Time Objective (RTO): The maximum acceptable duration of time that a system or application can be offline following a disaster."},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"Implementing an Automated Backup and DR Validation Script"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"To ensure your disaster recovery infrastructure is functioning correctly, continuous validation is necessary. Below is a Python script demonstrating how to verify cloud backup integrity and measure recovery readiness."},{"order":13,"type":"code","text":"import hashlib
import os

def verify_backup_integrity(file_path, expected_hash):
    sha256_hash = hashlib.sha256()
    if not os.path.exists(file_path):
        return False, "Backup file not found."
    
    with open(file_path, "rb") as f:
        for byte_block in iter(lambda: f.read(4096), b""):
            sha256_hash.update(byte_block)
            
    calculated_hash = sha256_hash.hexdigest()
    if calculated_hash == expected_hash:
        return True, "Integrity check passed."
    else:
        return False, "Integrity check failed. Backup may be corrupted."

# print(message)"},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practices for Cyber Resilience"},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Adopt the 3-2-1 Backup Rule: Maintain at least 3 copies of your data, across 2 different media types, with 1 copy stored offsite (or immutably in the cloud)."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Implement Immutable Backups: Protect backups from ransomware by making them write-once-read-many (WORM) so that administrative credentials cannot easily delete or encrypt them."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Regularly Test and Simulate: Conduct table-top exercises and full failover drills annually to validate RTO and RPO metrics under real-world pressure."}]
